clinicalPearls: Severe, early-onset hypertrophic demyelinating neuropathy of infancy or early childhood, historically termed HMSN III or CMT3.
A phenotypic severity label rather than a single gene: it arises from mutations in PMP22, MPZ, EGR2 or PRX, inherited as dominant de novo changes or as recessive disease.
Nerve conduction velocities are extremely slow, markedly lower than in typical CMT1.
Peripheral nerves are often palpably enlarged, and biopsy shows onion-bulb formations with hypomyelination.
Delayed motor milestones, severe distal and proximal weakness, sensory ataxia and generalised areflexia are characteristic.
Skeletal complications are prominent, including pes cavus, scoliosis and joint contractures; pupillary abnormalities are sometimes seen.
At its most severe it overlaps with congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy.
reference.pathophysiology: Dejerine-Sottas syndrome denotes the severe end of the hereditary demyelinating neuropathy spectrum and results from mutations in genes essential for peripheral myelin. The recognised causes are PMP22 (peripheral myelin protein 22), MPZ (myelin protein zero, P0), EGR2 (early growth response 2, a transcription factor that drives the Schwann cell myelination programme) and PRX (periaxin, required for the stability of mature myelin). Dominant de novo point mutations or biallelic recessive mutations in these genes severely disrupt the formation and maintenance of compact myelin, so that Schwann cells cannot myelinate normally. Repeated cycles of demyelination and attempted remyelination generate concentric onion-bulb whorls and nerve hypertrophy, while the profound loss of myelin produces the extreme slowing of conduction and the severe, early clinical deficit.
additionalDifferentials: Metachromatic leukodystrophy and Krabbe disease with infantile neuropathy
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography documenting markedly slowed velocities
Targeted gene panel covering PMP22, MPZ, EGR2 and PRX
Cerebrospinal fluid protein if an inflammatory neuropathy is being considered
Sural nerve biopsy showing onion bulbs and hypomyelination when genetics are inconclusive
Nerve ultrasound or MRI to demonstrate nerve hypertrophy
Ophthalmology and spinal assessment for associated deformity
redFlags: Respiratory muscle involvement or ventilatory compromise
Bulbar dysfunction with swallowing or airway difficulty
Rapid deterioration suggesting a superimposed acquired inflammatory neuropathy
Profound early hypotonia with feeding failure in infancy
reference.prognosis: Dejerine-Sottas syndrome causes severe, slowly progressive disability, with many affected individuals requiring walking aids or a wheelchair; life expectancy varies and is largely determined by the degree of respiratory involvement.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the disorder as chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy and giving prolonged immunotherapy.
Assuming a single causative gene rather than testing the full relevant panel.
Underestimating skeletal and respiratory complications that drive long-term morbidity.
Conflating this severe phenotype with milder CMT1 and giving falsely reassuring counselling.
